content: A giant congenital nevus is a dark-colored, often hairy patch of skin that is present at birth. In infants and children, it appears smaller but typically grows proportionally with the child. Once it stops growing, a giant pigmented nevus is defined as being larger than 8 inches in diameter. Symptoms of Giant Congenital Nevus A nevus presents as a dark-colored patch of skin, which may exhibit the following characteristics: A color ranging from brown to bluish-black. The presence of hair. Borders that may be regular or uneven. Possible small satellite areas around the main lesion. A skin surface that can be smooth, irregular, or wart-like in texture. These nevi are most commonly located on the upper or lower back or the abdomen. However, they may also appear on the arms, legs, mouth, mucous membranes, palms, or soles. Causes of Giant Congenital Nevus Bathing trunk nevi are believed to result from defects or abnormalities that occur during fetal development in the womb. In some families, these nevi may be inherited. They may also be associated with: Growth of fatty tissue cells (lipomas). Neurofibromatosis. Other nevi. Spina bifida. Smaller congenital pigmented or melanocytic nevi are more common in children and generally lead to fewer complications. Larger or giant nevi, however, are relatively rare. Risk Factors Giant congenital nevi occur in infants and are present at birth. Diagnosis All birthmarks should be evaluated by a healthcare provider. A skin biopsy may be performed to determine if the cells within the nevus have become cancerous. If the lesion is located over the spine, an MRI of the brain may be conducted, as there could be associated abnormalities in the brain. Physical Examination The physical examination of a giant pigmented nevus involves a detailed assessment of the skin lesion. This condition is often documented and studied using dermatology atlases. When to Seek Medical Care This condition is typically diagnosed at birth. Parents should schedule an appointment with a healthcare provider or mention it during a well-baby exam if their child has a large pigmented area on the skin. Treatment Options Treatment involves regular examinations to monitor for the development of skin cancers. When feasible, surgical removal of the nevus is performed. Skin grafting may be necessary in some cases. Larger nevi may require removal in multiple stages. Techniques such as laser therapy and dermabrasion can improve the cosmetic appearance of the nevus. However, these methods may not completely remove the birthmark and could complicate the diagnosis of skin cancer, such as melanoma. For these reasons, surgical intervention remains a controversial approach. Psychological support may also be beneficial to address the emotional impact of living with a disfiguring condition. Prognosis Skin cancer, including malignant melanoma and other types, may develop in up to 15% of individuals with larger or giant nevi, often during childhood. The risk is higher for nevi located on the back or abdomen. Possible Complications Depression and other emotional challenges due to the appearance of the nevus. Skin cancer, particularly melanoma. In rare cases, bathing trunk nevi may be associated with a condition called leptomeningeal melanocytosis, which involves the growth of pigment-producing cells in the brain or spinal cord.
